title: Ultrahigh strength magnesium via solidification of nanocolloid

paper_content.abstract: We report a simple, scalable route to produce ultrahigh-strength magnesium (Mg) via solidification of a colloidal solution containing nanoscale niobium carbide (NbC) particles suspended in liquid magnesium (Mg(l)). A single-atom-level investigation reveals that NbC exhibits spontaneous wetting with molten Mg, driven by the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface. This creates Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) particles in liquid Mg and is referred to as Mg(l)-Mg@NbC nanocolloid. This unique and spontaneous wetting behaviour enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion in the molten Mg without external fields, and in the solidified Mg matrix without the need for thermomechanical processing. The resulting NbC dispersoids act as coherent, hard reinforcement phases, significantly strengthening the Mg matrix. As a result, the Mg-NbC material exhibits ultrahigh tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing those of all previously reported Mg alloy systems.
paper_content.introduction:
Mg has a low density of 1.78 g·cm-3 and a high damping capacity with a loss factor ~11.8×10-3 (~10 times higher than Al and Steel), and thus offers tremendous potential in achieving lightweight vehicles with improved fuel economy and reduced CO emission.
2
However, the yield strengths of the most used automotive Mg alloys are in the range of 100-200 MPa, which is just nearly half that of Al alloys and 1/4 that of high strength steels; thus, the industry is not fully able to utilise their lightweight potential.
Among the major alloy strengthening mechanisms, the uniform dispersion of nanoscale secondary phase precipitates is particularly effective1. Alloying additions of rare earth (RE) elements in Mg alloys results in a significant strength improvement due to the effective precipitation of RE-containing phases upon heat treatment2, 3. Despite the promise of this approach, the high cost and limited availability of RE elements have historically hindered the widespread use of Mg-RE alloys in industry, with their potential only recently being actively explored4, 5.
As another strategy, fine-grained magnesium produced through thermomechanical processing is typically combined with precipitation hardening to achieve high strength6. However, the resulting microstructures often exhibit limited thermal stability, which compromises their performance under demanding service conditions.
Ceramic particles with high shear moduli, as an alternative approach to the in-situ formed precipitates, can serve as the non-deforming particles that favour the Orowan strengthening mechanism7. Their strengthening effect depends mainly on particle size and number density. This approach does not require specially tailored alloy compositions or complex thermomechanical processing routes. Reported data on various metallic systems highlight that in addition to ceramic particles contributing to strengthening8-12, the resulting nano-sized grain structure of the metallic matrix significantly improves the overall mechanical strength. For example, in Mg alloys, a multi-step external field treatment on molten metal followed by severe plastic deformation were conducted to disperse SiC nanoparticles13. In molybdenum alloys, the in-situ reaction of the precursor compounds14 was utilised to introduce the nano-sized ceramic particles and then a rolling process was conducted to disperse the nanoparticles and refine the Mo grain size. These ceramic phases are thermally stable and can effectively retain their strengthening effect at elevated temperatures. This is the case of Al incorporated with graphene-coated MgO nanoparticles9, via the powder metallurgy route, which showed improved strength and creep resistance at temperatures as high as 500°C. Similarly, non-equilibrium solidification in additive manufacturing was applied to incorporate La O nanoparticles in a medium entropy
2 3
alloy matrix and demonstrated further enhancement of creep property at 1093°C15
compared with the pure alloy parent phase.
We report here an ultrahigh tensile strength of ~680 MPa in Mg produced by solidification of a Mg colloid containing fine scale NbC dispersions. The favourable wetting characteristics of the NbC phase with molten magnesium enabled the processing of such high strength material. We investigate the fundamental mechanism for the atomic interaction between Mg and NbC using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). We further perform density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the interfacial interactions and atomic arrangements at the liquid Mg/NbC (Mg(l)/NbC) interfaces, with an emphasis on the non-polar NbC {001} surface that terminates most produced NbC nanoparticles. This study reveals that the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms, strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface, results in Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) colloid, which plays a critical role in the observed favourable wetting characteristics. During solidification of the Mg(l)-Mg@NbC colloid, the Mg solidification front spontaneously engulfs the NbC dispersoids into the growing Mg grains. In the resulting solidified alloys, these embedded dispersoids can effectively contribute to strengthening, similar to the role of coherent precipitates in monolithic Mg alloys.

We have identified the metal-ceramic (Mg-NbC) system as a promising candidate to realise this task, owing to its favourable wetting characteristics that enable the production of a high-temperature nanocolloidal solution consisting of NbC nano-dispersions in molten Mg using a simple, practical and scalable method.

NbC particle engulfment by the Mg solidification front
In typical solidification processes, ceramic particles (especially at the submicron or nanoscale) are often rejected at the solid/liquid interface due to interfacial energy considerations. This leads to particle segregation and clustering along grain boundaries, which can severely degrade the mechanical performance of the solidified metal. It is also notable that NbC possesses a significantly higher shear modulus (~230 GPa43) than in-situ formed precipitates44-47. These engulfed, chemically bonded high modulus NbC particles within the Mg matrix directly contribute to the effective strengthening48 of the Mg matrix.
In conclusion, this combined atomistic-level experimental and theoretical study reveals the formation of an ordered Mg layer bonded to NbC particles (Mg@NbC), which is responsible for the observed spontaneous wetting and engulfment. The resulting material exhibits high specific tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing many high-performance metals. To identify other metal-ceramic systems where the base molten metal spontaneously wets the ceramic nanoparticles, future design should specifically employ ab initio interface structure prediction and interfacial energy calculations. We believe DFT calculation can help in accelerating ceramic particle selection for metallic materials by investigating their interfacial interaction. Beyond magnesium, these insights provide a blueprint for designing next-generation structural and functional metal-ceramic systems and scalable nanocolloid-based processing.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript titled “Ultrahigh strength magnesium via solidification of nanocolloid” presents a comprehensive study on
Mg–NbC composites produced using NbC particles of varying sizes (nano, submicron, and micron). The work combines
solidification experiments, detailed electron microscopy, and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to investigate
colloidal stability and interfacial bonding. The technical depth and breadth of data presented, particularly in the
Supplementary Information, are impressive.
However, some critical issues need clarification:
1. The manuscript repeatedly compares the strengthenability of composites reinforced with different NbC particle sizes, but
this term is not rigorously defined. The key experimental comparison should focus on how the absolute mechanical
properties—yield strength, ductility, and modulus—evolve with particle size and volume fraction. If “strengthenability” refers
to strengthening efficiency, the authors must clearly define the normalization basis (e.g., per particle surface area, interface
volume, or particle-matrix load transfer coefficient).
2. Given that the authors invoke Mg@NbC coating and CNbC-like interfacial layers, the particle-size dependence should
naturally be linked to surface-to-volume ratio and interfacial energetics. Yet, no direct evidence or quantitative discussion of
how surface energy or bonding characteristics evolve with particle size is provided. A clear correlation between AIMD-
derived interface stability and experimental mechanical performance is missing.
3. Table S2 shows that the NbC volume fraction increases dramatically with particle size—from 12% (nano) to ~54%
(micron). This large variation introduces a confounding factor: it is unclear whether the observed strengthening trend arises
primarily from particle size, particle fraction, or both. A normalization or controlled comparison (e.g., constant volume fraction)
would help isolate the dominant strengthening mechanism.
4. The manuscript attributes strength enhancement to size effects and interface ordering, yet contributions from grain
refinement, load transfer, and dislocation–particle interactions are not separated. Clarification through composite modeling
or a rule-of-mixtures comparison would enhance the credibility of the claims.
5. The paper is data-rich but difficult to navigate. The key mechanistic insights—particularly the transition from colloidal
stability to interface-controlled strengthening—should be summarized more clearly within the main text rather than being
deferred to supplementary sections.
Overall, this is a technically strong and potentially impactful study, but the mechanistic rationale linking particle size,
interface stability, and mechanical strengthening can be improved.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper presents an innovative approach to producing ultrahigh-strength magnesium by infiltrating molten Mg into a pellet
of NbC nanoparticles. It combined atomic-scale experimental evidence and first-principles DFT simulations to demonstrate
the spontaneous wetting and coherent bonding at the Mg/NbC interface. The fabrication method is fairly straight forward. A
uniform dispersion of NbC nanoparticles without relying on external fields or complex thermomechanical processing was
achieved.
However, the powder pellet method is somewhat difficult to scale up for large scale production. The pellet method may limit
its flexibility of NbC particle volume percent. Long-term thermal stability of the Mg-NbC composites will be of interest.
Overall, it is a plausible paper with merit.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have undertaken a very interesting study on the role of dispersed nano-particles on the properties of Mg, which
they are calling a nano-colloid. This has been the challenge with nano-composites, i.e. how to achieve a homogeneous
dispersion of nano-particles, rather than finding them in clusters. I am aware of such processes having been used previously
to create nano-composites. Some of the challenge can be when these pellets are added to melts particularly with gravity
separation because normally lower levels of particles are preferred.
One of the drawbacks of this paper is that it compares the properties of these materials with standard alloys. However, what
is shown here are metal matrix compositions with a very large amount of the second phase. The volume % are 12, 39 and
54%, however it should be realised that given the density different the mass% is a lot greater. This is the primary reason for
the increase in modulus and hardness, i.e. that is it not really a Mg based material, it is primarily a ceramic. Having said that
the nano-particle version still is majority Mg although it is still high enough content to be a metal matrix composite and
should be compared with other MMCs. So comparison with similar materials is required.
I also do not believe that the micro-tensile tests are providing a useful comparison of the properties. Samples at this size are
well below critical flaw sizes and consequently do not give a reasonable estimate of the tensile properties that can be
expected in typical use cases. Nor should these results be compared with results from macro-tensile tests. The failure is
completely different as shown by the tensile curve results. The failure is seen in Supp Fig 7 which is interesting but not
helpful for comparision with bulk properties. The real tensile data is observed in Supplementary Fig 2 which is very different.
So comparison of materials in the same or similar test is required.
I think that when appropriate materials and testing methods are compared the properties shown are not as outstanding as it
appears.
There is a nice microscopic and DFT study of the interface indicating that there is templating on the particles as has been
described previously by researchers from Brunel in this group. Whilst DFT is a useful tool, it is not the only tool to
understanding the interface behaviour. The conclusions indicate that DFT can predict the wetting behaviour of metals on
ceramic nano-particles. It is not clear to me that NbC was chosen because of the these calculations. If not, I would be
interested in seeing results that backed that statement up more strongly.

## Abstract

We report a simple, scalable route to produce ultrahigh-strength magnesium (Mg) via solidification of a colloidal solution containing nanoscale niobium carbide (NbC) particles suspended in liquid magnesium (Mg(l)). A single-atom-level investigation reveals that NbC exhibits spontaneous wetting with molten Mg, driven by the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface. This creates Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) particles in liquid Mg and is referred to as Mg(l)-Mg@NbC nanocolloid. This unique and spontaneous wetting behaviour enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion in the molten Mg without external fields, and in the solidified Mg matrix without the need for thermomechanical processing. The resulting NbC dispersoids act as coherent, hard reinforcement phases, significantly strengthening the Mg matrix. As a result, the Mg-NbC material exhibits ultrahigh tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing those of all previously reported Mg alloy systems.

---

## Introduction

Mg has a low density of 1.78 g·cm-3 and a high damping capacity with a loss factor ~11.8×10-3 (~10 times higher than Al and Steel), and thus offers tremendous potential in achieving lightweight vehicles with improved fuel economy and reduced CO emission.
2
However, the yield strengths of the most used automotive Mg alloys are in the range of 100-200 MPa, which is just nearly half that of Al alloys and 1/4 that of high strength steels; thus, the industry is not fully able to utilise their lightweight potential.
Among the major alloy strengthening mechanisms, the uniform dispersion of nanoscale secondary phase precipitates is particularly effective1. Alloying additions of rare earth (RE) elements in Mg alloys results in a significant strength improvement due to the effective precipitation of RE-containing phases upon heat treatment2, 3. Despite the promise of this approach, the high cost and limited availability of RE elements have historically hindered the widespread use of Mg-RE alloys in industry, with their potential only recently being actively explored4, 5.
As another strategy, fine-grained magnesium produced through thermomechanical processing is typically combined with precipitation hardening to achieve high strength6. However, the resulting microstructures often exhibit limited thermal stability, which compromises their performance under demanding service conditions.
Ceramic particles with high shear moduli, as an alternative approach to the in-situ formed precipitates, can serve as the non-deforming particles that favour the Orowan strengthening mechanism7. Their strengthening effect depends mainly on particle size and number density. This approach does not require specially tailored alloy compositions or complex thermomechanical processing routes. Reported data on various metallic systems highlight that in addition to ceramic particles contributing to strengthening8-12, the resulting nano-sized grain structure of the metallic matrix significantly improves the overall mechanical strength. For example, in Mg alloys, a multi-step external field treatment on molten metal followed by severe plastic deformation were conducted to disperse SiC nanoparticles13. In molybdenum alloys, the in-situ reaction of the precursor compounds14 was utilised to introduce the nano-sized ceramic particles and then a rolling process was conducted to disperse the nanoparticles and refine the Mo grain size. These ceramic phases are thermally stable and can effectively retain their strengthening effect at elevated temperatures. This is the case of Al incorporated with graphene-coated MgO nanoparticles9, via the powder metallurgy route, which showed improved strength and creep resistance at temperatures as high as 500°C. Similarly, non-equilibrium solidification in additive manufacturing was applied to incorporate La O nanoparticles in a medium entropy

alloy matrix and demonstrated further enhancement of creep property at 1093°C15

We report here an ultrahigh tensile strength of ~680 MPa in Mg produced by solidification of a Mg colloid containing fine scale NbC dispersions. The favourable wetting characteristics of the NbC phase with molten magnesium enabled the processing of such high strength material. We investigate the fundamental mechanism for the atomic interaction between Mg and NbC using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). ## Abstract

We report a simple, scalable route to produce ultrahigh-strength magnesium (Mg) via solidification of a colloidal solution containing nanoscale niobium carbide (NbC) particles suspended in liquid magnesium (Mg(l)). A single-atom-level investigation reveals that NbC exhibits spontaneous wetting with molten Mg, driven by the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface. This creates Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) particles in liquid Mg and is referred to as Mg(l)-Mg@NbC nanocolloid. This unique and spontaneous wetting behaviour enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion in the molten Mg without external fields, and in the solidified Mg matrix without the need for thermomechanical processing. The resulting NbC dispersoids act as coherent, hard reinforcement phases, significantly strengthening the Mg matrix. As a result, the Mg-NbC material exhibits ultrahigh tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing those of all previously reported Mg alloy systems.

## Introduction

Mg has a low density of 1.78 g·cm-3 and a high damping capacity with a loss factor ~11.8×10-3 (~10 times higher than Al and Steel), and thus offers tremendous potential in achieving lightweight vehicles with improved fuel economy and reduced CO emission.
2
However, the yield strengths of the most used automotive Mg alloys are in the range of 100-200 MPa, which is just nearly half that of Al alloys and 1/4 that of high strength steels; thus, the industry is not fully able to utilise their lightweight potential.
Among the major alloy strengthening mechanisms, the uniform dispersion of nanoscale secondary phase precipitates is particularly effective1. Alloying additions of rare earth (RE) elements in Mg alloys results in a significant strength improvement due to the effective precipitation of RE-containing phases upon heat treatment2, 3. Despite the promise of this approach, the high cost and limited availability of RE elements have historically hindered the widespread use of Mg-RE alloys in industry, with their potential only recently being actively explored4, 5.
As another strategy, fine-grained magnesium produced through thermomechanical processing is typically combined with precipitation hardening to achieve high strength6. However, the resulting microstructures often exhibit limited thermal stability, which compromises their performance under demanding service conditions.
Ceramic particles with high shear moduli, as an alternative approach to the in-situ formed precipitates, can serve as the non-deforming particles that favour the Orowan strengthening mechanism7. Their strengthening effect depends mainly on particle size and number density. This approach does not require specially tailored alloy compositions or complex thermomechanical processing routes. Reported data on various metallic systems highlight that in addition to ceramic particles contributing to strengthening8-12, the resulting nano-sized grain structure of the metallic matrix significantly improves the overall mechanical strength. For example, in Mg alloys, a multi-step external field treatment on molten metal followed by severe plastic deformation were conducted to disperse SiC nanoparticles13. In molybdenum alloys, the in-situ reaction of the precursor compounds14 was utilised to introduce the nano-sized ceramic particles and then a rolling process was conducted to disperse the nanoparticles and refine the Mo grain size. These ceramic phases are thermally stable and can effectively retain their strengthening effect at elevated temperatures. This is the case of Al incorporated with graphene-coated MgO nanoparticles9, via the powder metallurgy route, which showed improved strength and creep resistance at temperatures as high as 500°C. Similarly, non-equilibrium solidification in additive manufacturing was applied to incorporate La O nanoparticles in a medium entropy

alloy matrix and demonstrated further enhancement of creep property at 1093°C15

We report here an ultrahigh tensile strength of ~680 MPa in Mg produced by solidification of a Mg colloid containing fine scale NbC dispersions. The favourable wetting characteristics of the NbC phase with molten magnesium enabled the processing of such high strength material. NbC particle engulfment by the Mg solidification front
In typical solidification processes, ceramic particles (especially at the submicron or nanoscale) are often rejected at the solid/liquid interface due to interfacial energy considerations. This leads to particle segregation and clustering along grain boundaries, which can severely degrade the mechanical performance of the solidified metal. In contrast, as shown in Supplementary Figs. 2b, 4c, 6c, the Mg-NbC system surprisingly exhibited uniform particle dispersions with a wide range of particle sizes (from nanoscale to microscale) in the entire solidified Mg matrix, indicating a favourable interfacial interaction. In conclusion, this combined atomistic-level experimental and theoretical study reveals the formation of an ordered Mg layer bonded to NbC particles (Mg@NbC), which is responsible for the observed spontaneous wetting and engulfment. The resulting material exhibits high specific tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing many high-performance metals. To identify other metal-ceramic systems where the base molten metal spontaneously wets the ceramic nanoparticles, future design should specifically employ ab initio interface structure prediction and interfacial energy calculations. We believe DFT calculation can help in accelerating ceramic particle selection for metallic materials by investigating their interfacial interaction. Beyond magnesium, these insights provide a blueprint for designing next-generation structural and functional metal-ceramic systems and scalable nanocolloid-based processing.

## Abstract

We report a simple, scalable route to produce ultrahigh-strength magnesium (Mg) via solidification of a colloidal solution containing nanoscale niobium carbide (NbC) particles suspended in liquid magnesium (Mg(l)). A single-atom-level investigation reveals that NbC exhibits spontaneous wetting with molten Mg, driven by the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface. This creates Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) particles in liquid Mg and is referred to as Mg(l)-Mg@NbC nanocolloid. This unique and spontaneous wetting behaviour enables uniform nanoparticle dispersion in the molten Mg without external fields, and in the solidified Mg matrix without the need for thermomechanical processing. The resulting NbC dispersoids act as coherent, hard reinforcement phases, significantly strengthening the Mg matrix. As a result, the Mg-NbC material exhibits ultrahigh tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing those of all previously reported Mg alloy systems.

## Introduction

Mg has a low density of 1.78 g·cm-3 and a high damping capacity with a loss factor ~11.8×10-3 (~10 times higher than Al and Steel), and thus offers tremendous potential in achieving lightweight vehicles with improved fuel economy and reduced CO emission.
2
However, the yield strengths of the most used automotive Mg alloys are in the range of 100-200 MPa, which is just nearly half that of Al alloys and 1/4 that of high strength steels; thus, the industry is not fully able to utilise their lightweight potential.
Among the major alloy strengthening mechanisms, the uniform dispersion of nanoscale secondary phase precipitates is particularly effective1. Alloying additions of rare earth (RE) elements in Mg alloys results in a significant strength improvement due to the effective precipitation of RE-containing phases upon heat treatment2, 3. Despite the promise of this approach, the high cost and limited availability of RE elements have historically hindered the widespread use of Mg-RE alloys in industry, with their potential only recently being actively explored4, 5.
As another strategy, fine-grained magnesium produced through thermomechanical processing is typically combined with precipitation hardening to achieve high strength6. However, the resulting microstructures often exhibit limited thermal stability, which compromises their performance under demanding service conditions.
Ceramic particles with high shear moduli, as an alternative approach to the in-situ formed precipitates, can serve as the non-deforming particles that favour the Orowan strengthening mechanism7. Their strengthening effect depends mainly on particle size and number density. This approach does not require specially tailored alloy compositions or complex thermomechanical processing routes. Reported data on various metallic systems highlight that in addition to ceramic particles contributing to strengthening8-12, the resulting nano-sized grain structure of the metallic matrix significantly improves the overall mechanical strength. For example, in Mg alloys, a multi-step external field treatment on molten metal followed by severe plastic deformation were conducted to disperse SiC nanoparticles13. In molybdenum alloys, the in-situ reaction of the precursor compounds14 was utilised to introduce the nano-sized ceramic particles and then a rolling process was conducted to disperse the nanoparticles and refine the Mo grain size. These ceramic phases are thermally stable and can effectively retain their strengthening effect at elevated temperatures. This is the case of Al incorporated with graphene-coated MgO nanoparticles9, via the powder metallurgy route, which showed improved strength and creep resistance at temperatures as high as 500°C. Similarly, non-equilibrium solidification in additive manufacturing was applied to incorporate La O nanoparticles in a medium entropy
2 3
alloy matrix and demonstrated further enhancement of creep property at 1093°C15
compared with the pure alloy parent phase.
We report here an ultrahigh tensile strength of ~680 MPa in Mg produced by solidification of a Mg colloid containing fine scale NbC dispersions. The favourable wetting characteristics of the NbC phase with molten magnesium enabled the processing of such high strength material. We investigate the fundamental mechanism for the atomic interaction between Mg and NbC using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). We further perform density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the interfacial interactions and atomic arrangements at the liquid Mg/NbC (Mg(l)/NbC) interfaces, with an emphasis on the non-polar NbC {001} surface that terminates most produced NbC nanoparticles. This study reveals that the formation of an ordered layer of Mg atoms, strongly bonded to the carbon atoms on the NbC {001} surface, results in Mg-coated NbC (Mg@NbC) colloid, which plays a critical role in the observed favourable wetting characteristics. During solidification of the Mg(l)-Mg@NbC colloid, the Mg solidification front spontaneously engulfs the NbC dispersoids into the growing Mg grains. In the resulting solidified alloys, these embedded dispersoids can effectively contribute to strengthening, similar to the role of coherent precipitates in monolithic Mg alloys.

NbC particle engulfment by the Mg solidification front
In typical solidification processes, ceramic particles (especially at the submicron or nanoscale) are often rejected at the solid/liquid interface due to interfacial energy considerations. This leads to particle segregation and clustering along grain boundaries, which can severely degrade the mechanical performance of the solidified metal. In contrast, as shown in Supplementary Figs. 2b, 4c, 6c, the Mg-NbC system surprisingly exhibited uniform particle dispersions with a wide range of particle sizes (from nanoscale to microscale) in the entire solidified Mg matrix, indicating a favourable interfacial interaction. In conclusion, this combined atomistic-level experimental and theoretical study reveals the formation of an ordered Mg layer bonded to NbC particles (Mg@NbC), which is responsible for the observed spontaneous wetting and engulfment. The resulting material exhibits high specific tensile strength and stiffness, surpassing many high-performance metals. To identify other metal-ceramic systems where the base molten metal spontaneously wets the ceramic nanoparticles, future design should specifically employ ab initio interface structure prediction and interfacial energy calculations. We believe DFT calculation can help in accelerating ceramic particle selection for metallic materials by investigating their interfacial interaction. Beyond magnesium, these insights provide a blueprint for designing next-generation structural and functional metal-ceramic systems and scalable nanocolloid-based processing.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript titled “Ultrahigh strength magnesium via solidification of nanocolloid” presents a comprehensive study on
Mg–NbC composites produced using NbC particles of varying sizes (nano, submicron, and micron). The work combines
solidification experiments, detailed electron microscopy, and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to investigate
colloidal stability and interfacial bonding. The technical depth and breadth of data presented, particularly in the
Supplementary Information, are impressive.
However, some critical issues need clarification:
1. The manuscript repeatedly compares the strengthenability of composites reinforced with different NbC particle sizes, but
this term is not rigorously defined. The key experimental comparison should focus on how the absolute mechanical
properties—yield strength, ductility, and modulus—evolve with particle size and volume fraction. If “strengthenability” refers
to strengthening efficiency, the authors must clearly define the normalization basis (e.g., per particle surface area, interface
volume, or particle-matrix load transfer coefficient).
2. Given that the authors invoke Mg@NbC coating and CNbC-like interfacial layers, the particle-size dependence should
naturally be linked to surface-to-volume ratio and interfacial energetics. Yet, no direct evidence or quantitative discussion of
how surface energy or bonding characteristics evolve with particle size is provided. A clear correlation between AIMD-
derived interface stability and experimental mechanical performance is missing.
3. Table S2 shows that the NbC volume fraction increases dramatically with particle size—from 12% (nano) to ~54%
(micron). This large variation introduces a confounding factor: it is unclear whether the observed strengthening trend arises
primarily from particle size, particle fraction, or both. A normalization or controlled comparison (e.g., constant volume fraction)
would help isolate the dominant strengthening mechanism.
4. The manuscript attributes strength enhancement to size effects and interface ordering, yet contributions from grain
refinement, load transfer, and dislocation–particle interactions are not separated. Clarification through composite modeling
or a rule-of-mixtures comparison would enhance the credibility of the claims.
5. The paper is data-rich but difficult to navigate. The key mechanistic insights—particularly the transition from colloidal
stability to interface-controlled strengthening—should be summarized more clearly within the main text rather than being
deferred to supplementary sections.
Overall, this is a technically strong and potentially impactful study, but the mechanistic rationale linking particle size,
interface stability, and mechanical strengthening can be improved.

with a very large amount of the second phase. The volume % are 12, 39 and 54%, however
it should be realised that given the density different the mass% is a lot greater. This is the
primary reason for the increase in modulus and hardness, i.e. that is it not really a Mg based
material, it is primarily a ceramic. Having said that the nano-particle version still is majority
Mg although it is still high enough content to be a metal matrix composite and should be
compared with other MMCs. So comparison with similar materials is required.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that materials with high reinforcement volume
fractions should be compared primarily with other metal matrix composites. To address this
point, we have expanded the comparative framework in the revised manuscript.
Specifically, we have collated data from the literature on Mg-, Al-, Ti-, and Fe-based metal
matrix composites reinforced with oxides, carbides, borides, and nitrides, which is now
presented in Supplementary Tables 1 and 3. A direct comparison between these established
MMC systems and the present Mg-NbC materials is provided as inset in Fig. 2b. This
comparison shows that, even when benchmarked against other MMCs with comparable
reinforcement levels, the Mg-NbC system processed using simple solidification process
exhibits remarkable improvement in yield strength. The dataset in Fig. 2d compares strength
and modulus relative to density of a range of alloys and their composites.
R3.2. I also do not believe that the micro-tensile tests are providing a useful comparison of
the properties. Samples at this size are well below critical flaw sizes and consequently do
not give a reasonable estimate of the tensile properties that can be expected in typical use
cases. Nor should these results be compared with results from macro-tensile tests. The
failure is completely different as shown by the tensile curve results. The failure is seen in
Supp Fig 7 which is interesting but not helpful for comparison with bulk properties. The real
tensile data is observed in Supplementary Fig 2 which is very different. So comparison of
materials in the same or similar test is required.
I think that when appropriate materials and testing methods are compared the properties
shown are not as outstanding as it appears.
Response: We agree that micro-tensile and macro-tensile tests probe different aspects of
mechanical behaviour and should be interpreted accordingly. We have clarified this
distinction more explicitly in the revised manuscript. In the section “Ultrahigh tensile strength
in Mg-NbC materials” on page 6, the Fig.2 has been modified and expanded by adding new
results, and the corresponding text is also revised.
In this work, micro-tensile testing (Fig. 2a) was intentionally performed on materials with a
single-crystal Mg matrix, both without particles and with dispersed NbC particles. This design
allows a direct and controlled comparison of the intrinsic strengthening effect of NbC
particles on Mg deformation, while eliminating contributions from grain boundaries and, texture. In this context, the micro-tensile results are not intended to represent bulk
engineering properties, but rather to reveal the fundamental strengthening capability of the
Mg-NbC system at the crystal level.
In contrast, newly added Fig. 2b includes two distinct datasets: (i) micro-tensile results
obtained from Mg-NbC material (square symbol), and (ii) macro-tensile results obtained from
polycrystalline Mg-NbC materials (diamond symbol) containing submicron and micron-sized
NbC particles, following ASTM E8 standard. These macro-tensile results reflect bulk
mechanical behaviour and incorporate the effects of grain structure, particle distribution, and
processing-induced defects.
The two testing approaches are used in a complementary manner (micro-tensile tests
establish the intrinsic, upper-bound strengthening potential arising from particle-matrix
interactions, while macro-tensile tests demonstrate the translation of this potential to bulk,
polycrystalline materials at realistic length scales). The yield strength improvement
measured in macro and micro-tensile experiments are consistent with the theoretical
predicted tendency for all particle size and volume fraction. Dataset in Fig. 2b, provide a
coherent picture of mechanical response at both local and bulk Mg-NbC materials.
R3.3. There is a nice microscopic and DFT study of the interface indicating that there is
templating on the particles as has been described previously by researchers from Brunel in
this group. Whilst DFT is a useful tool, it is not the only tool to understanding the interface
behaviour. The conclusions indicate that DFT can predict the wetting behaviour of metals on
ceramic nano-particles. It is not clear to me that NbC was chosen because of the these
calculations. If not, I would be interested in seeing results that backed that statement up
more strongly.
Response: We first experimentally observed the exceptional wetting characteristic and
colloidal stability of NbC in liquid Mg. The ab initio molecular dynamics simulations were
subsequently performed to rationalise and interpret this experimentally observed
phenomenon at the atomic scale. The simulations reveal the formation of ordered Mg-C
interfacial bonding and provide a quantitative measure of interfacial stability, supporting the
experimental observations. We believe DFT calculation can help in accelerating ceramic
phase selection for metallic materials by investigating the formation of ordered layer on
ceramic phase as one of the necessary conditions to realise the excellent wetting of the
molten metal to the ex-situ incorporated ceramic phases.
